stories.title: 18 Year-Old from the Bronx Starts Nonprofit to Sponsor School Children in Ghana
stories.summary: At 15, Max Owobu started spending summers in Ghana and saw kids his age working instead of going to school. So he started the Yenko Foundation with his allowance — and now, as a Bronx high school senior, he's sponsoring children's K-5 education with meals, tuition, and uniforms.
stories.extended_summary: Max Owobu was 15 the first time he spent a summer in Ghana, the country of his Nigerian father's upbringing. What stuck with him: kids his own age selling things on the street or working in family shops, not in classrooms. Back home in the Bronx, he started the Yenko Foundation with money he'd saved from his weekly allowance — enough to send one child, Matthew, to school. Now a high school senior juggling prom, exams, and college applications, Max runs a 501(c)3 that sponsors K-5 education in Ghana, covering tuition, school meals, and uniforms. In a city where scam schools charge parents hundreds for glorified daycare, his foundation is the real thing.

stories.title: OSU Chemistry Breakthrough, And Maybe a Greener Future for Semiconductors and Atomic Energy
stories.summary: Separating zirconium from hafnium is one of the hardest splits on the periodic table — and the current method burns millions of pounds of toxic, flammable solvent every year. Oregon State chemists patented a water-based alternative that could green up semiconductors and nuclear power.
stories.extended_summary: Zirconium and hafnium are nearly identical twins on the periodic table — which is exactly why separating them at high purity is so brutally hard, and so essential for microelectronics and nuclear reactors. Only two U.S. facilities can do it at industrial scale, each burning millions of pounds of flammable organic solvent annually and losing about 4 percent of it into the air as pollution. Oregon State University chemists Alex Roseborough and May Nyman patented a water-based process instead, potentially cutting the environmental cost of a separation that underpins both the semiconductor and atomic energy industries.
